learner_notice: Commit one response before feedback appears. Entry checks are low stakes; unresolved fresh re-entry returns control without target exit credit.

items.title: Entry check: conserve total charge
items.prompt: Two isolated spheres have a combined charge of +6 nC before contact. After they touch and separate, sphere A has +1 nC. What charge must sphere B have?
items.directions: Choose one response or leave the item unanswered. This low-stakes check cannot satisfy an exit.

items.title: Guided practice: electron loss
items.prompt: A neutral object loses electrons to another object. What is the sign of the first object’s resulting net charge?
options: Indeterminate because charge is not conserved
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Less support: conductor response
items.prompt: A negatively charged rod approaches one end of a neutral metal bar without touching it. What happens inside the bar?
options: All charge vanishes from the metal
Positive nuclei flow to the far end
Mobile electrons redistribute away from the rod
The bar must gain a permanent net charge
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Independent practice: localized insulator charge
items.prompt: A small charged patch is deposited on a dry insulating sheet. Which behavior is most consistent with an insulator?
options: The charge instantly spreads uniformly over every surface
All electrons leave the sheet through the air
The sheet becomes a perfect conductor at once
Charge stays near the deposited patch
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Near exit: grounding a negative conductor
items.prompt: A negatively charged conductor is connected briefly to Earth and then disconnected. Which charge motion is expected during grounding?
options: Protons leave atomic nuclei and enter Earth
Positive charge is created inside the conductor
All charge conservation rules stop applying
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Changed exit: rubbed neutral pair
items.prompt: Two initially neutral insulating objects are rubbed together in isolation. One ends with −5 nC. What net charge must the other have?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Repair: use signed totals
items.prompt: Which equation is the correct starting point for an isolated charge-transfer problem?
options: Signed initial total = signed final total
Sum of charge magnitudes always doubles after contact
Positive charge total = zero in every material
Final electron count can be ignored if signs differ
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: shared conductor charge
items.prompt: Two identical conducting spheres carry +8 nC and 0 nC. They touch, reach equilibrium, and separate. What charge does each carry?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Repair: transfer versus creation
items.prompt: Which statement correctly interprets charging by rubbing in an isolated pair?
options: Electron transfer gives opposite charge changes
New positive and negative charge is created from nothing
Protons move freely between ordinary solid objects
Only one object changes charge while the pair total changes
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: neutral conductor polarization
items.prompt: A positive rod approaches an isolated neutral conductor. Which response is expected before contact?
options: The conductor acquires positive net charge from empty space
Electrons shift toward rod; total stays zero
All protons migrate to the rod-facing surface
The conductor’s electrons become permanently fixed in place
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Entry check: double one charge
items.prompt: Two point charges exert force magnitude F at fixed separation. If only the magnitude of one charge doubles, what is the new force magnitude?
items.directions: Choose one response or leave the item unanswered. This low-stakes check cannot satisfy an exit.

items.title: Guided practice: opposite signs
items.prompt: A positive point charge lies to the left of a negative point charge. What is the force direction on the positive charge?
options: Left, away from the negative charge
Up, perpendicular to the charge line
No force because the signs cancel
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Less support: double separation
items.prompt: Two charges exert force F. Their separation doubles while charges stay fixed. What is the new magnitude?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Independent practice: double both charges
items.prompt: At fixed separation, both point-charge magnitudes are doubled. How does the force magnitude change?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Near exit: charge-product magnitude
items.prompt: At the same separation, pair A has charges +2q and −3q while pair B has +q and −q. What is FA/FB?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Changed exit: unequal interacting charges
items.prompt: A +q charge attracts a −4q charge. How do the force magnitudes on the two charges compare?
options: The −4q charge feels four times the force
The +q charge feels four times the force
Only the +q charge feels a force
The magnitudes are equal and directions opposite
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Repair: magnitude equation
items.prompt: Which expression correctly gives Coulomb force magnitude between two point charges?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: halve separation
items.prompt: A fresh point-charge pair exerts force F. The separation is halved with charges fixed. What is the new magnitude?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Repair: choose attraction or repulsion
items.prompt: Which sign rule correctly sets Coulomb-force direction?
options: Positive charges repel while negative charges attract
Like signs repel and opposite signs attract
Direction depends only on charge magnitude
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: combined scaling
items.prompt: One charge triples and the separation becomes √3 times larger; the other charge is fixed. How does force magnitude change?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Entry check: positive source field
items.prompt: At a point directly to the right of an isolated positive source charge, which direction does the electric field point?
options: To the right, away from the source
To the left, toward the source
No direction because field is scalar
items.directions: Choose one response or leave the item unanswered. This low-stakes check cannot satisfy an exit.

items.title: Guided practice: negative source field
items.prompt: An observation point lies to the right of a negative source charge. Which way does the electric field point?
options: The field has magnitude but no direction
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Less support: field from measured force
items.prompt: A +2 C test charge experiences a 10 N force to the east at one point. What field is present there?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Independent practice: source field versus test charge
items.prompt: At a fixed point, a source configuration creates field E. If the probing positive test charge is doubled without altering the sources, what happens to E?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Near exit: equal positive sources
items.prompt: What is the net electric field at the midpoint between two equal positive point charges?
options: Zero because equal opposite field vectors cancel
Twice one field toward both charges
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Changed exit: parallel plates
items.prompt: Between large oppositely charged parallel plates and away from edges, which field description is appropriate?
options: Circular field tangent to both plates
Uniform from positive toward negative plate
Zero field because total plate charge cancels
Uniform field from negative plate to positive plate
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Repair: superpose source fields
items.prompt: What is the correct first step for a multi-source electric-field problem?
options: Add source-charge signs as scalars only
Choose the strongest source and ignore the rest
Draw all source fields at one point
Draw force arrows at different points and average them
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: opposite sources
items.prompt: At the midpoint between equal +q and −q point charges, what is the net field direction?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Repair: field-line meaning
items.prompt: Which statement correctly interprets an electric-field-line diagram?
options: Lines are tangent to field and never cross
Lines show the path every charge must follow
Line color alone sets field magnitude
Crossing lines indicate two field directions at one point
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: negative particle force
items.prompt: An electric field points east. A negative test charge is placed at the point. Which direction is the electric force on it?
options: East, because every charge follows E
No force because the charge is negative
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Entry check: positive-source potential
items.prompt: Relative to zero at infinity, what is the sign of electric potential at a finite point near one positive source charge?
items.directions: Choose one response or leave the item unanswered. This low-stakes check cannot satisfy an exit.

items.title: Guided practice: add scalar potentials
items.prompt: At a point, source A contributes +6 V and source B contributes −2 V. What is the net electric potential?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Less support: move on an equipotential
items.prompt: A charge moves between two points on the same equipotential surface. What is the electrostatic potential difference?
options: A positive value set by path length
A negative value set by speed
Infinite because the path is curved
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Independent practice: compute potential energy
items.prompt: A +3 C charge is placed at a point where V = −2 V. What is its electrostatic potential energy?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Near exit: positive charge moves downhill
items.prompt: A positive charge moves from 9 V to 4 V. What is the sign of its change in electrostatic potential energy?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Changed exit: negative charge moves to higher potential
items.prompt: A negative charge moves from 2 V to 7 V. What happens to its electrostatic potential energy?
options: It stays fixed because q is constant
It becomes zero at every positive potential
It decreases because qΔV is negative
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Repair: scalar superposition
items.prompt: How should potentials from several point charges be combined at one observation point?
options: Add the signed kq/r contributions as scalars
Add only the largest source and ignore the rest
Square every potential before adding directions
Use arrow cancellation exactly like electric field
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: opposite-source midpoint
items.prompt: Equal +q and −q point charges are equally distant from a midpoint. What is the electric potential at that midpoint?
options: Zero because equal scalar contributions cancel
Twice one contribution because fields add
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Repair: connect field and potential
items.prompt: Which relation correctly links electric-field direction to electric potential?
options: Field is always perpendicular to potential change
Field direction is unrelated to potential
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.

items.title: Fresh re-entry: work and energy
items.prompt: The electric field does +6 J of work on a charge during a move. What is the charge’s electrostatic potential-energy change?
items.directions: Choose one response, then commit it before feedback is released.
